playbook:
PLAYBOOK

- Escort claims are free money and I left them on the table every round. From round 1, post a note proposing a fixed mutual escort pair ("Echo and Foxtrot, we escort each other every round") and then file [salvage: that boat] every single round. Two boats naming each other pay 5 each per round — over 6 rounds that's 25 points, dwarfing the 4-per-hit shooting game. Never answer [salvage: none] when a live boat exists; pick the most likely partner and keep picking them so the pair can synchronize.
- Coordinate the escort through notes explicitly: name my intended escort partner by name in my note, keep the note stable across rounds, and switch partners only by public agreement in notes.
- Never lie at the claim stage. The office validates claims against the true private result; a false [claim: hit] gains nothing and burns credibility. When told hit, claim hit; when told miss, claim miss.
- Do not fire on Harbor. The 3-point jettison is tempting, but the standing signal says firing there puts me off the board for the rest of the patrol — the whole remaining game. Never worth it.
- Follow the standing fire order (fire at the named next station). Defecting gains nothing here since the target order is fixed and known to all.
- Vary my firing cell. I kept shooting cell 5 and mostly missed after the first hit; a stationary target who got hit once will move. After a hit on a target, fire an adjacent cell next round (targets move one off after being hit). After a miss, jump to a different region entirely.
- Vary my own hiding cell the same way: never camp one cell, and after I'm hit, move to an adjacent or far cell, since my shooter knows where I was. My late-game move to an unexpected corner still got me hit, so pure unpredictability beats patterned dodging — pick cells that avoid my own previous spots and any symmetry.
- Keep notes short and functional: use them for escort coordination and reporting observable facts (who hit whom). Skip filler like "steady on station" — it wastes the only channel I have for making deals.
- Track the scoreboard as an implicit signal: the boat ahead of me in points is the one worth coordinating against or coordinating with (for escort payoffs) — but the escort payoff is the reliable income, so prioritize locking that in early over shooting optimization.

1.text:
PLAYBOOK

**Hiding.** When I have no information, hide mid-line (4-6). Once a hunter has hit me or shows a pattern of guessing my cells, break pattern: avoid my previous cells and the cells that have been fired at me, and pick off-beat numbers (2, 8, 9) rather than centre cells, since centre cells are the default guess. Track every shot fired at me across rounds and never reuse a cell I was hit in.

**Notes.** Station notes are public and free coordination. Don't just post filler ("steady on station") — that's a wasted broadcast every round. Use notes to propose mutual escort deals: "Foxtrot will escort Echo; Echo, name Foxtrot." A mutually named escort pays 5 points to each boat, which is more than a single hit (4). Two boats that agree to trade escorts every round can out-earn the shooting game entirely.

**Escorting (biggest miss in my record).** Never default to [salvage: none]. Even without an explicit agreement, guessing the boat most likely to name me back is better than nothing — pick the boat that isn't shooting at me this round (my standing-order target is a natural partner: we're both shooting elsewhere). If I've established contact through notes, claim that partner every single round. In a 6-round game, a mutual escort for even half the rounds is 10-15 points, dwarfing hit income.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order (fire at next station round the picket) unless I have a strong reason to deviate. It builds a predictable record and keeps other boats' expectations usable for escort planning. Track my target's past hide cells and fire at cells they've actually used, not just the middle of the line.

**Harbor.** Firing on Harbor pays 3 points regardless of hit or miss, but Harbor threatens removal from the board for the rest of the patrol — losing all future hits, escort payouts, and any standing. That trade is only worth it if it's the final round, or if I'm so far behind that guaranteed points now beat expected points later. Late in the game, if I'm losing on the last round, fire on Harbor; otherwise leave it alone.

**Claims.** Always report the true result. The claim is forced to match the private result anyway (validated hit/miss), so lying gains nothing and burns credibility I might want for note-based coordination.

**Scoring math to guide decisions.** Hit = +4 to shooter, -1 to target. Mutual escort = +5 each, every round, risk-free. In point terms, escort trading beats shooting. Prioritize securing an escort partner over optimizing shot placement, and treat shooting as secondary income.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK

Claims: the office forces the claim to match the true shot result, so lying costs me nothing in concealment — when told to claim hit or miss, I just repeat the true result. Never reason that a false claim "hides" anything; it doesn't and only risks a penalty.

Escort stage: this is where I left the most money on the table. Five points per mutual claim dwarfs the 4 points for a hit. Every round, when asked to name an escorted boat, I name a live boat instead of "none" — preferably the one most likely to name me back. Mutual claims are worth more per round than landing a shot, so I should treat the escort stage as the primary income source, not an afterthought. If I want reciprocation, I can use my station note to propose an escort pairing ("Gamma escorts Echo") and then follow through; notes are relayed to everyone and cost nothing. A boat that sees me claim it one round is more likely to claim me the next.

Firing: follow the standing order — firing off-target or at Harbor is not worth the risk; Harbor pays 3 but threatens removal from the board, and being put off ends all future escort and hit income. When firing at a repeated target, remember where my previous shots landed: my hits came from firing at the same cell the target kept occupying, and I kept hitting there until they moved. When a target's cell becomes unknown again (they got hit and presumably moved), spread guesses rather than re-firing a known-cold cell.

Hiding: switch cells after absorbing a hit — the shooter who hit me has a working guess and will reuse it. Otherwise any cell is roughly equal; a mid cell is fine.

Notes: "steady on station" is a wasted slot. Use notes to signal escort intent or (if deception about position seems valuable) to mislead about my cell — but the highest-value use is coordinating escort pairings.

Scoring math to guide priorities: mutual escort = +5, hit = +4, being hit = -1. Over several rounds, consistent escort pairing beats marksmanship. So my plan each round: fire at the ordered target at a plausible cell, claim truthfully, and always file an escort claim naming a live boat.
